hypothesis: If Darwin's claim holds, the late Chalk (latter part of the Secondary/Mesozoic) lies roughly 300 million years or more in the past, so the numeric age of the top of the Chalk-bearing Cretaceous System in the modern geological time scale is at or above about 300 Ma.
pass_criterion: The International Chronostratigraphic Chart gives the top of the Cretaceous (Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, end of the Maastrichtian) an age of at least 250 Ma, so that 'far more than 300 million years since the latter part of the Secondary' is consistent with the data.
fail_criterion: The chart gives the end-Cretaceous boundary an age below 150 Ma, i.e. less than half of Darwin's figure. The expected value is about 66 Ma, and the youngest Chalk (Maastrichtian) is about 72-66 Ma. Ages from 150 to 250 Ma are scored as inconclusive and as not confirming the claim.
interpretation: 'Secondary period' maps to the Mesozoic Era. 'Latter part of the Secondary period / late Chalk' maps to the Upper Cretaceous (Chalk Group, about 100-66 Ma). 'Years elapsed since' maps to the numeric age in Ma of the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, the end of Chalk deposition. Darwin's denudation arithmetic is a rate-based estimate of elapsed time. The test compares it with the radiometrically and astronomically calibrated age of the boundary. It does not measure denudation itself, which is a deliberate modern reinterpretation. Fields used: unit name (Cretaceous, Upper Cretaceous, Maastrichtian) and numeric base/top ages in Ma.

dataset.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart
dataset.why_it_fits: It is the official numeric time scale, with ages in Ma for every stage boundary, downloadable as PDF and in machine-readable form. It gives the end of the Cretaceous (about 66 Ma) and the Upper Cretaceous stages, so it can be compared with Darwin's roughly 300 Ma.
